What happens if your economy is suddenly in crisis, Brussels offers help with strings attached—and Turkey, China or Russia can move faster? What if your country delivers every reform the EU asks for, only for a member state to block the next step anyway? And after years of waiting, would voters still choose to join?

In this special bonus episode, The Neighbourhood goes live from Lisbon for an EU enlargement game.Jessica Hendrickbrings together RE-ENGAGE experts representing six EU candidate countries and throws a series of fictional—but very plausible—political and economic shocks at them inspired by real headlines: Russia’s intensified attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, Ireland’s EU presidency push on enlargement, Iceland’s referendum, Germany’s regional elections and the upcoming 2026 Enlargement Package. Drawing on three years of surveys, interviews and crisis simulations, each expert has to answer for their country.

The result is part enlargement simulation, part policy conversation and part game night. The experts bargain over a fictional €100 million EU cheque, decide whether the EU can compete with faster offers from other powers, test how easily disinformation could exploit frustration with enlargement, and imagine what would happen if EU membership was finally put to a public vote. item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
The geopolitics of trade

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-09-18

The rules that have governed global trade for decades are now under more pressure than at any point since they were written. Tariffs are back as a frontline political weapon.

Major economies are pouring money into industrial policy. The WTO's dispute settlement mechanism has been effectively paralysed for years. And the assumption that deeper economic integration would produce political stability is being openly questioned by governments across the political spectrum.

So how are governments and firms adapting to this world where trade is inseparable from geopolitics?

What rules and dynamics are emerging from this period of disruption?

And what kind of global trade governance, if any, are we moving toward?

In this episode of the NUPI podcast The World Stage, NUPI Senior Research Fellow Taylor St John sits down with Arancha González, Dean of the Paris School of International Affairs at Sciences Po to discuss these questions.

item.content:encoded:
How do diplomats work with technology?

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-09-18

Lars Gjesvik from NUPI argues that his research shows the decisions made about AI diplomacy today will shape the field for decades to come.

The earliest traces of diplomacy go back several thousand years. Since then, the topics discussed and negotiated between countries have grown steadily in number and become far more complex.

In recent decades, technology has pushed its way more firmly onto the diplomatic agenda. One of the clearest examples is the way cyber diplomacy has developed into a distinct branch of diplomacy. This has created opportunities for diplomats, but also challenges.

In a new research article published in the prestigious journal International Affairs, Senior Research Fellow Lars Gjesvik from NUPI and Associate Professor Ole Willers from Copenhagen Business School write about diplomacy in the age of expertise.

When diplomats set out to discuss new technologies, a range of new problems arise. Technology affects every area of society, it can be hard to understand, and it develops quickly. So when digital technology became a diplomatic issue in earnest, a series of questions surfaced:

The way these challenges were resolved for cyber diplomacy tells a story in itself. But it also points to how today's pressing topics, such as artificial intelligence (AI), should be approached.

That is the argument of the two researchers behind the article “Diplomacy in the age of expertise: the case of cyber diplomacy”.

We study how political institutions, political processes  and political action shape and are shaped by democracy and rights, economic outcomes and social development.

Rule of law, civil liberties and basic political rights are under threat in countries worldwide.

Our research focuses on the growing pressure against democratic institutions in Africa. We have cooperated closely with African partners for decades and have extensive fieldwork experience.

Our research holds high academic quality and provides concrete input to actors engaged in bilateral work, and to donors and activists navigating the shrinking space for civil society.
